Everything in this walkthrough runs. The expensive fits use cache_fit(), which saves the result in cache/. The first run estimates the model and later runs load the saved fit. Delete the corresponding cache file only when you deliberately want to refit a changed model.

install.packages(c("netify", "blockmodels", "igraph", "NetMix", "ggplot2", "reshape2", "patchwork", "dplyr", "coda", "digest", "scales", "remotes"))
remotes::install_github("s7minhas/lame")

1 What We Are Trying to Understand Today

Day 8 was about constructing defensible network data. Day 9 asks what we can learn once the same actors appear in many relationships, which means those relationships are connected rather than independent rows. We will compare several ways to represent the patterns that our measured variables miss.

  1. The social relations model (SRM) asks whether some actors repeatedly appear in more relationships than their measured characteristics would lead us to expect.
  2. The additive and multiplicative effects model (AME) keeps those broad actor patterns and asks whether particular pairs still fit together unusually well or unusually poorly.
  3. Blockmodels ask whether actors follow a small number of recurring relationship patterns, first in one observed network and then across repeated networks.

The applications are real. The cross-sectional analysis uses tactical cooperation among Syrian armed organizations collected by Gade et al. (2019). The longitudinal analysis uses annual Integrated Crisis Early Warning System (ICEWS) material-conflict networks and a repeated-network mixed-membership model implemented in NetMix. The broader NetMix framework can model hidden Markov dynamics, but our fast classroom specification estimates separate annual memberships without a transition process.

ImportantThe Thread That Connects the Models

We are not collecting methods for their own sake. We are asking what part of the story is still missing after the measured variables enter. Is it that some actors are broadly involved, that particular pairs work together unusually well, or that actors occupy a few recurring relational roles? Each model represents one of those possibilities.

1.1 The Applied Model Compass

Model Research question What the model adds Plain-language interpretation
Independent dyadic regression Which observed characteristics are associated with cooperation? A familiar first comparison “A useful first look, but it acts as if ANF-ASIM tells us nothing about ANF-ISIL.”
SRM Which organizations cooperate unusually often across many partnerships? One adjusted activity score per organization “ANF and ASIM took part in more joint operations across their partnerships than their measured characteristics would lead us to expect.”
AME Which pairs cooperate unusually well after broad actor activity enters? One or more hidden pair-pattern factors “Some pairs worked together unusually often even after we account for each organization’s overall activity.”
Cross-sectional SBM Does cooperation follow a few recurring relational roles? A role for each organization and a cooperation rate for each role pairing “ANF and ASIM form a small tactical core with links across a much larger, sparsely connected periphery.”
Longitudinal SRM Which states repeatedly appear on the source and target sides of high-volume coded events? One adjusted source-side and target-side score per state “Some states repeatedly appear in many high-volume coded event pairs, on both the source and target sides.”
Repeated-network NetMix How does each state’s pattern of relationships look in each year? A yearly blend of roles for each state “A state’s high-volume connections can be broad in some years and narrow in others without placing it in a permanent camp.”

2 A Real Network: Cooperation in the Syrian Rebellion

Gade et al. (2019) ask a direct question: with whom do armed organizations cooperate in a fragmented civil war? They assembled claims of joint tactical operations from July 2012 through June 2015 and measured ideological distance, power differences, shared operational location, and common state sponsorship. Their broader data collection began with more than 9,000 claims of attacks. The prepared regression table available here contains 30 organizations with complete covariates; the observed binary network used for the block analysis contains the 31 organizations that recorded at least one cooperative relationship.

The dependent variable is the number of claimed joint operations for each pair. It is symmetric because a joint operation belongs to the pair rather than traveling from a sender to a receiver. We follow the published analysis and use the square root of the count. The transformation makes the very skewed counts more compatible with a Gaussian working model and keeps the classroom analysis close to the published application. Ideological distance runs from 0 to 4, power is recorded in thousands of estimated fighters, and shared location and sponsorship are binary. Current versions of lame also support an overdispersed Poisson family, which would be an appropriate sensitivity model for a new paper.

load("data/gade_app.rda")
gade <- data
rm(data)
gade$sqrt_coop <- sqrt(gade$coopActions)
checkpoint(actors = length(unique(gade$actor1)), directed_rows = nrow(gade), observed_pairs = nrow(gade) / 2, cooperative_pairs = sum(gade$coopActions > 0) / 2)
#> ------------------------------------------------------------------
#> CHECKPOINT: actors = 30   |   directed_rows = 870   |   observed_pairs = 435   |   cooperative_pairs = 85
#> ------------------------------------------------------------------
head(gade[, c("actor1", "actor2", "coopActions", "ideol_diff", "powerdiff", "loc", "spons")])
actor1 actor2 coopActions ideol_diff powerdiff loc spons
2 13th 101st 1 0.0000000 0.2 1 1
3 AARB 101st 0 0.3333333 7.0 1 0
4 ASIM 101st 1 1.8333333 13.0 1 0
5 AASG 101st 0 1.5566667 1.0 0 0
6 AF 101st 0 0.0000000 8.0 1 0
7 1st 101st 0 0.3333333 1.1 1 1

The duplicated directions are a storage convention. Because the relationship is symmetric, A-B and B-A carry the same outcome and covariates. The model counts each unordered pair once.

2.1 Start With the Expectations

  • If ideological compatibility helps organizations coordinate tactics and agree about long-term goals, greater ideol_diff should be associated with less cooperation.
  • If organizations seek similarly powerful partners, greater powerdiff should be associated with less cooperation.
  • Organizations operating in the same location have more opportunities to conduct joint operations, so loc should be positively associated with cooperation.
  • If shared external patrons coordinate their clients, spons should be positively associated with cooperation. The published study does not find clear evidence for this last expectation.

These are associational expectations. The data are observational, and ideology, power, location, sponsorship, and cooperation may affect one another. A network model changes the dependence assumptions. It does not create random assignment.

3 Put the Data Into the Form the Model Needs

gade_net <- netify(
  input = gade,
  actor1 = "actor1", actor2 = "actor2",
  symmetric = TRUE, weight = "sqrt_coop",
  nodal_vars = c("averageId_actor1", "size_actor1", "spons_actor1"),
  dyad_vars = c("ideol_diff", "powerdiff", "loc", "spons"),
  dyad_vars_symmetric = rep(TRUE, 4),
  missing_to_zero = TRUE
)
gade_lame <- to_lame(gade_net, family = "normal")
Yg <- gade_lame$Y
Xg <- gade_lame$Xdyad
Ng <- gade_lame$Xrow
dim(Yg)
#> [1] 30 30
dim(Xg)
#> [1] 30 30  4
colnames(Ng)
#> [1] "averageId_actor1" "size_actor1"      "spons_actor1"

Yg is a symmetric 30 by 30 matrix. Xg is a 30 by 30 by 4 dyadic-covariate array. Ng contains one row per organization. The diagonal of Yg is missing because an organization cannot conduct a joint operation with itself.

NoteWhat Changes in a Directed Network?

This application is symmetric, so each organization receives one additive actor effect. In a directed network, such as one state directing a threat toward another, the SRM separates the source side from the target side:

yij=𝐱ij𝖳𝛃+ai+bj+ϵij,(aibi)∼𝒩[(00),(σa2σabσabσb2)],Corr(ϵij,ϵji)=ρ. \begin{aligned} y_{ij}&=\mathbf{x}_{ij}^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta+a_i+b_j+\epsilon_{ij},\\ \begin{pmatrix}a_i\\b_i\end{pmatrix} &\sim\mathcal N\!\left[ \begin{pmatrix}0\\0\end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix}\sigma_a^2&\sigma_{ab}\\\sigma_{ab}&\sigma_b^2\end{pmatrix} \right],\qquad \operatorname{Corr}(\epsilon_{ij},\epsilon_{ji})=\rho . \end{aligned}

Here aia_i records how often actor ii appears on the source side beyond the measured predictors, while bib_i records how often the same actor appears on the target side. The variances σa2\sigma_a^2 and σb2\sigma_b^2 describe how much those adjusted source-side and target-side scores differ across actors. The covariance σab\sigma_{ab} asks whether actors that are often sources are also often targets. The residual correlation ρ\rho asks a different question: after the actor effects and predictors enter, is an unexpectedly high i→ji\!\rightarrow\!j outcome paired with an unexpectedly high j→ij\!\rightarrow\!i outcome? The label iid\mathrm{iid} means independent and identically distributed across actors. The symmetric model is not a lesser model. It matches the meaning of a joint operation.

4 Why Independent Dyads Are the Wrong Benchmark

An independent dyadic regression says

yij=β0+𝐱ij𝖳𝛃+𝐰i𝖳𝛄+𝐰j𝖳𝛄+ϵij,ϵij∼iidN(0,σ2). y_{ij} = \beta_0 + \mathbf{x}_{ij}^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta + \mathbf{w}_i^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\gamma + \mathbf{w}_j^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\gamma + \epsilon_{ij}, \qquad \epsilon_{ij} \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} N(0,\sigma^2).

The intercept β0\beta_0 is the baseline. The vector 𝐱ij\mathbf x_{ij} contains measured pair attributes and 𝛃\boldsymbol\beta their coefficients. The vectors 𝐰i\mathbf w_i and 𝐰j\mathbf w_j contain measured organization attributes and 𝛄\boldsymbol\gamma their coefficients. The error ϵij\epsilon_{ij} is what remains unique to the pair. The label iid\mathrm{iid} means independent and identically distributed: every pair error is assumed to be a separate draw from the same normal distribution.

The conditional mean is sensible, but the IID statement says that evidence from ANF-ASIM is unrelated to evidence from ANF-ISIL, even though both relationships involve ANF. If ANF is unusually cooperative for reasons we did not measure, all pairs involving ANF will lean in the same direction.

4.1 Return the Residuals to the Network

gade_pair_id <- apply(gade[, c("actor1", "actor2")], 1, function(x) paste(sort(x), collapse = "|"))
gade_unique <- gade[!duplicated(gade_pair_id), ]
gade_unique$ideology_sum <- gade_unique$averageId_actor1 + gade_unique$averageId_actor2
gade_unique$size_sum <- gade_unique$size_actor1 + gade_unique$size_actor2
gade_unique$sponsor_sum <- gade_unique$spons_actor1 + gade_unique$spons_actor2
glm_gade <- lm(sqrt_coop ~ ideology_sum + size_sum + sponsor_sum + ideol_diff + powerdiff + loc + spons, data = gade_unique)
summary(glm_gade)$coefficients[c("ideol_diff", "powerdiff", "loc", "spons"), ]
#>               Estimate Std. Error    t value     Pr(>|t|)
#> ideol_diff -0.10050790 0.03863771 -2.6012902 9.609940e-03
#> powerdiff  -0.04883364 0.01006541 -4.8516298 1.719223e-06
#> loc         0.28927955 0.10038600  2.8816722 4.155213e-03
#> spons      -0.02863539 0.13554526 -0.2112608 8.327846e-01
Eg <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow(Yg), ncol(Yg), dimnames = dimnames(Yg))
for (ii in seq_len(nrow(gade_unique))) {
  a <- gade_unique$actor1[ii]
  b <- gade_unique$actor2[ii]
  Eg[a, b] <- Eg[b, a] <- resid(glm_gade)[ii]
}
actor_resid <- sort(rowMeans(Eg, na.rm = TRUE), decreasing = TRUE)
head(actor_resid, 8)
#>       ASIM        ANF        SAS       AASG        1st         LH        ASB 
#> 1.31095878 0.90988048 0.15861814 0.13836235 0.10410700 0.10174776 0.08682228 
#>        ASL 
#> 0.08358004
sd(actor_resid)
#> [1] 0.3522839

If the independent model had absorbed the recurring-actor structure, these means would hover near zero. Instead, the same organizations repeatedly appear above or below the regression line.

5 The Symmetric Social Relations Model

The SRM adds one latent effect for every organization:

yij=β0+𝐱ij𝖳𝛃+𝐰i𝖳𝛄+𝐰j𝖳𝛄+ai+aj+ϵij,ai∼iidN(0,σa2). y_{ij} = \beta_0 + \mathbf{x}_{ij}^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta + \mathbf{w}_i^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\gamma + \mathbf{w}_j^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\gamma + a_i + a_j + \epsilon_{ij}, \qquad a_i \stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} N(0,\sigma_a^2).

Each organization gets one effect, aia_i, and that same effect appears in every partnership involving the organization. A positive value means the organization took part in more joint operations across its partners than the model expected. The variance σa2\sigma_a^2 summarizes how much organizations differ from one another in this overall adjusted activity. The distribution also partially pools the organization estimates toward zero, so they are not simply raw cooperation counts.

For a directed network, replace ai+aja_i+a_j with ai+bja_i+b_j. The model then estimates sender variance, receiver variance, their covariance, and dyadic reciprocity. Back and Kenny (2010) provide the general SRM decomposition; Hoff (2005) develops the network regression version; Minhas et al. (2022) show why these components matter for network inference.

6 The Inference Issue: Three Cases, Not One Slogan

A missing factor can move a coefficient up or down. The direction depends on two questions. Does the missing factor increase or decrease cooperation? Is it more common when the measured predictor is high or low?

Let xijx_{ij} be a measured predictor such as ideological distance, and let zijz_{ij} be a missing process such as shared command infrastructure or unmeasured brokerage. Suppose the true model is

yij=βxij+γzij+ϵij, y_{ij} = \beta x_{ij} + \gamma z_{ij} + \epsilon_{ij},

but we regress yy only on xx. In the linear case, the omitted-variable calculation is

plim(β̂naive)=β+γCov(x,z)Var(x). \operatorname{plim}(\widehat\beta_{\text{naive}}) = \beta + \gamma\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(x,z)}{\operatorname{Var}(x)}.

The probability limit, plim\operatorname{plim}, is the value an estimate approaches as the sample becomes very large. Here β\beta is the association we want for xx, while γ\gamma describes how the missing process zz relates to cooperation. The equation gives us three distinct cases.

Relationship between measured xx and omitted zz What happens to the point estimate? What can still go wrong?
Positive covariance If γ>0\gamma>0, the estimate for xx is pulled upward Some of the missing process is mistakenly credited to xx
Negative covariance If γ>0\gamma>0, the estimate for xx is pulled downward and can cross zero A weak or negative estimate can hide a more positive direct association
Zero covariance The estimate for xx can remain centered on β\beta If zz contains recurring actor effects, the usual uncertainty calculation can still be wrong because pairs sharing actors remain connected

The sign reverses if γ<0\gamma<0. With several measured predictors, the relevant overlap is what remains between xx and zz after accounting for the other included variables. “Networks make coefficients biased” is therefore too crude. A coefficient can be centered correctly even when the usual uncertainty calculation is wrong. Coefficient bias appears when the missing process both matters for the outcome and overlaps with the predictor.

6.1 A Concrete Reading

Imagine that ideological distance is our measured xx and that the missing process zz raises cooperation. If ideologically similar organizations are also more likely to share command infrastructure, leaving that infrastructure out can make ideological similarity look more important than the conditional association we would estimate if the infrastructure were measured. If brokers deliberately connect ideologically distant groups, leaving brokerage out can make ideological distance look less negatively associated with cooperation than it would if brokerage were measured. The algebra tells us why the same missing process can move the ideology estimate in opposite directions.

The algebra tells us the direction conditional on assumptions. The data do not reveal the sign of an unmeasured covariance by themselves.

ImportantWhat an SRM Does Not Magically Solve

The SRM accounts for patterns shared by pairs involving the same actor. It does not turn observational data into a causal design. If an unmeasured actor or pair process overlaps with a measured predictor, the coefficient can still blend the two explanations.

Useful responses include measuring the missing process, adding each actor’s long-run predictor average in a correlated-random-effects or Mundlak specification, separating change within an actor from differences across actors, comparing actor fixed effects when the question permits it, and checking whether the conclusion survives a richer AME model. Time-invariant actor variables cannot receive separate coefficients from actor fixed effects in one cross-section.

Minhas et al. (2022) make the boundary especially clear. When the omitted dependency is independent of the observed predictor and has a recoverable low-rank structure, AME can recover the coefficient and the latent dependency well in simulation. If z=αx+ez=\alpha x+e, however, the naive coefficient targets the combined association β+γα\beta+\gamma\alpha. No latent-variable method can recover β\beta as a separate direct effect without additional assumptions.

7 Baby Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC): How the Model Is Estimated

The model must learn the measured-variable coefficients, each organization’s activity effect, how much those effects vary overall, and eventually the hidden pair-pattern factors. Instead of trying to settle everything at once, the sampler takes turns.

  1. Start with provisional values.
  2. Update the measured-variable coefficients while temporarily holding the actor effects fixed.
  3. Update every organization’s actor effect using its observed partnerships and the current coefficients.
  4. Update how much the actor effects and leftover errors vary overall.
  5. When AME factors are included, update those hidden pair-pattern coordinates and their scale.
  6. Repeat, discard the early settling-in rounds, and use the later saved rounds to describe uncertainty.

A chain is a connected walk through plausible parameter values for one observed network. It is not a collection of newly observed Syrian conflicts. A trace plot should show stable fuzzy movement rather than a continuing trend or a stuck line. Effective sample size translates the saved, correlated rounds into the rough number of independent draws carrying the same information. These are useful warning checks, not proof that the model or interpretation is correct. One chain is enough to show the classroom mechanics, while a research analysis should compare independently started chains and verify that the result survives them.

8 Fit the Independence Model and SRM

gade_indep <- cache_fit("gade_indep_v2", ame(
  Y = Yg, Xdyad = Xg, Xrow = Ng,
  family = "normal", symmetric = TRUE,
  nvar = FALSE, R = 0, seed = 6886,
  nscan = 10000, burn = 10000, odens = 10,
  verbose = FALSE
))
gade_srm <- cache_fit("gade_srm_v2", ame(
  Y = Yg, Xdyad = Xg, Xrow = Ng,
  family = "normal", symmetric = TRUE,
  nvar = TRUE, R = 0, seed = 6886,
  nscan = 10000, burn = 10000, odens = 10,
  verbose = FALSE
))

In these calls, nscan sets the number of MCMC updates, burn sets how many early updates are discarded while the chain settles, and odens saves every tenth later update. Saving every tenth draw reduces storage; it does not manufacture new information.

The only modeling switch is nvar: FALSE treats the pairs as independent conditional on the covariates, while TRUE estimates one persistent organization effect. R = 0 says there are no multiplicative latent factors yet.

trace_plot(gade_srm)
round(coda::effectiveSize(coda::mcmc(gade_srm$BETA)))
#>             intercept averageId_actor1_node      size_actor1_node 
#>                  1000                  1000                  1000 
#>     spons_actor1_node       ideol_diff_dyad        powerdiff_dyad 
#>                  1000                  1000                  1000 
#>              loc_dyad            spons_dyad 
#>                  1000                  1000

round(cbind(independent = b_ind, srm = b_srm, lo = ci_srm[, 1], hi = ci_srm[, 2]), 3)

The point estimates suggest less cooperation as ideological and power differences grow, more cooperation among organizations operating in the same location, and no clear shared-sponsorship pattern. The uncertainty is not equally decisive. In the SRM, the power-difference interval stays below zero, while the ideology, location, and sponsorship intervals cross zero. The estimates are on the square-root count scale, so they should not be narrated as percentage changes. The comparison shows which patterns survive persistent organizational activity rather than licensing a stronger causal story.

Do not reduce the comparison to “the standard errors got wider.” Both point estimates and interval widths can move, and they need not move in the same direction. The new model changes the conditional mean by adding the actor effects and changes the covariance structure by recognizing repeated organizations.

8.2 The Actor Effects Tell Us About Organizations

# APM stores the posterior mean additive actor effect for each organization.
gade_effects <- data.frame(actor = names(gade_srm$APM), effect = as.numeric(gade_srm$APM))
gade_effects <- gade_effects[order(gade_effects$effect), ]
tail(gade_effects, 8)
actor effect
16 ATB 0.0690359
9 AFB 0.0773224
26 LH 0.0886674
6 AASG 0.0943339
15 ASL 0.0993324
29 SAS 0.1687062
11 ANF 0.8108279
14 ASIM 1.1173601 
ggplot(gade_effects, aes(effect, reorder(actor, effect))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey70") +
  geom_point(color = "#18453B", size = 2.5) +
  labs(x = "Adjusted cooperative-activity effect", y = NULL)

Al-Nusrah Front (ANF) and Ahrar al-Sham Islamic Movement (ASIM) receive the two highest adjusted cooperation scores in this fit. ANF was an al-Qaeda-affiliated sectarian-jihadist organization during this period, while ASIM was a major Salafist-nationalist organization. Both recorded more joint operations across their partnerships than their measured ideology, size, sponsorship, and location would lead the model to expect. This does not mean either organization was inherently cooperative. The high values could reflect capacity, battlefield reach, brokerage, geography, reporting, or some combination of these. The plot shows posterior mean scores for this network and period, not uncertainty intervals for each organization.

Minhas et al. (2022) use the same logic in international conflict. Their reanalysis of Reiter and Stam shows that sender effects identify countries that initiate more or fewer disputes than the observed covariates predict. The latent effects become clues about missing explanations, not merely nuisance controls.

9 Use the SRM as a Latent-Variable Tool

The additive effect aia_i is already latent, meaning we infer it from the pattern of relationships rather than observe it directly. It can be used in two ways.

  1. A fuller model of recurring actors: include aia_i so the measured variables do not have to explain every recurring difference among organizations. This helps with the dependence problem but does not guarantee that actor effects are unrelated to the predictors.
  2. A clue worth following: inspect which organizations repeatedly sit above or below the model’s prediction, compare that pattern with outside information, and ask what mechanism the measured variables missed.

That second use requires humility. The model shows us a repeated pattern that our measured variables missed. It cannot tell us by itself whether the explanation is capacity, brokerage, geography, reporting, or something else. Giving the effect a name requires evidence beyond the fitted network.

9.1 From One Latent Number per Actor to Latent Affinities

The SRM can tell us that an organization records more cooperation across its partnerships. AME can also tell us that it works especially often with a particular set of partners. It learns that pair-specific pattern from the network after accounting for the measured variables and each organization’s overall activity:

yij=β0+𝐱ij𝖳𝛃+𝐰i𝖳𝛄+𝐰j𝖳𝛄+ai+aj+𝐮i𝖳𝐃𝐮j+ϵij. y_{ij} = \beta_0+\mathbf{x}_{ij}^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta+\mathbf{w}_i^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\gamma+\mathbf{w}_j^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\gamma+a_i+a_j+\mathbf{u}_i^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{u}_j+\epsilon_{ij}.

The vector 𝐮i\mathbf u_i is organization ii’s unobserved relational profile. The diagonal matrix 𝐃\mathbf D weights the profile dimensions when organizations ii and jj meet. Their product, 𝐮i𝖳𝐃𝐮j\mathbf{u}_i^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{u}_j, lets particular pairings be fitted higher or lower than their measured characteristics and broad actor activity would suggest. In technical language, it can represent unmeasured homophily, clustering, or stochastic equivalence. Hoff (2005) introduced the bilinear mixed-effects formulation for dyadic data. Minhas, Hoff, and Ward (2019) develop AME as an inferential framework for networks. Gade et al. (2019) use it for this Syrian cooperation application.

gade_ame <- cache_fit("gade_ame_r1_v3", ame(
  Y = Yg, Xdyad = Xg, Xrow = Ng,
  family = "normal", symmetric = TRUE, nvar = TRUE,
  R = 1, seed = 6886,
  nscan = 10000, burn = 10000, odens = 10,
  verbose = FALSE
))

R is the number of hidden pair-pattern factors, also called the rank. R = 1 adds the smallest possible multiplicative layer. We use it as the main fit because one factor is already enough to reproduce the observed tendency for cooperation to cluster in threes. We also fit two factors to see whether the conclusions depend on that choice.

gade_ame_r2 <- cache_fit("gade_ame_r2_v2", ame(
  Y = Yg, Xdyad = Xg, Xrow = Ng,
  family = "normal", symmetric = TRUE, nvar = TRUE,
  R = 2, seed = 6886,
  nscan = 10000, burn = 10000, odens = 10,
  verbose = FALSE
))
focal_terms <- c("ideol_diff_dyad", "powerdiff_dyad", "loc_dyad", "spons_dyad")
summarize_focal <- function(fit, model) {
  intervals <- t(apply(fit$BETA[, focal_terms, drop = FALSE], 2, quantile, c(.025, .975)))
  data.frame(model = model, term = focal_terms, estimate = colMeans(fit$BETA)[focal_terms], interval_low = intervals[, 1], interval_high = intervals[, 2], row.names = NULL)
}
ame_rank_comparison <- do.call(rbind, list(
  summarize_focal(gade_indep, "Independent dyads"),
  summarize_focal(gade_srm, "SRM"),
  summarize_focal(gade_ame, "AME, rank 1"),
  summarize_focal(gade_ame_r2, "AME, rank 2")
))
ame_rank_comparison[-c(1, 2)] <- round(ame_rank_comparison[-c(1, 2)], 3)
ame_rank_comparison

The power-difference and shared-location conclusions survive both ranks: similarly powerful organizations and organizations operating in the same location record more joint operations after the other included terms and latent structure enter. Ideology is more sensitive. Its interval stays below zero at rank one but crosses zero at rank two, even though both fits reproduce the targeted third-order statistic. The published analysis reports a clearer ideology result, but our current-package reanalysis shows that the precision of that conclusion depends on how much latent structure we ask the model to absorb. That sensitivity is part of the result, not an inconvenience to conceal.

Show the priors used by the main AME fit 
prior_summary(gade_ame)

This fit uses the current data-scaled defaults in lame. Those defaults, the current package version, and the rank choice need not reproduce the historical AMEN implementation exactly. We therefore call this a classroom reanalysis of the same application, not an exact numerical replication of every published estimate.

9.2 Put the Coefficients Back Into Joint Operations

The coefficients act on the fitted square root of the operation count. To make that scale concrete, take an otherwise fixed dyad whose fitted square-root count is 2 and use four operations as a simple back-transformed reference because 22=42^2=4. We apply each retained rank-one coefficient draw to that reference point. This is a scale illustration, not a claim that the expected count equals the square of the transformed-scale expectation.

ame_delta <- cbind(
  "Ideology gap: 0 to 2 points" = 2 * gade_ame$BETA[, "ideol_diff_dyad"],
  "Power gap: 0 to 10,000 fighters" = 10 * gade_ame$BETA[, "powerdiff_dyad"],
  "Different to shared location" = gade_ame$BETA[, "loc_dyad"]
)
ame_count_change <- (2 + ame_delta)^2 - 4
ame_action_summary <- data.frame(
  comparison = colnames(ame_count_change),
  reference_operations = 4,
  back_transformed_operations = round((2 + apply(ame_delta, 2, median))^2, 2),
  change_lo = round(apply(ame_count_change, 2, quantile, .025), 2),
  change_hi = round(apply(ame_count_change, 2, quantile, .975), 2)
)
ame_action_summary
comparison reference_operations back_transformed_operations change_lo change_hi
Ideology gap: 0 to 2 points Ideology gap: 0 to 2 points 4 3.56 -0.77 -0.08
Power gap: 0 to 10,000 fighters Power gap: 0 to 10,000 fighters 4 3.38 -1.10 -0.04
Different to shared location Different to shared location 4 4.63 0.09 1.18

At the four-operation reference, the rank-one fit moves the back-transformed scale to about 3.56 operations for a two-point ideology gap, 3.38 for a 10,000-fighter power gap, and 4.63 for shared operational location. The ideology interval changes across the rank sensitivity, while the power and location directions remain stable. Squaring a conditional mean on the transformed scale is not the same as computing a full posterior expected count, so these are deliberately modest scale illustrations. They are not predictions for a named pair, causal effects, or a claim that every dyad begins with four operations.

9.3 Check the Main Rank From Another Starting Point

gade_ame_check <- cache_fit("gade_ame_r1_seed1729_v1", ame(
  Y = Yg, Xdyad = Xg, Xrow = Ng,
  family = "normal", symmetric = TRUE, nvar = TRUE,
  R = 1, seed = 1729,
  nscan = 10000, burn = 10000, odens = 10,
  verbose = FALSE
))
round(cbind(seed_6886 = colMeans(gade_ame$BETA)[focal_terms], seed_1729 = colMeans(gade_ame_check$BETA)[focal_terms]), 3)
#>                 seed_6886 seed_1729
#> ideol_diff_dyad    -0.056    -0.057
#> powerdiff_dyad     -0.016    -0.015
#> loc_dyad            0.151     0.148
#> spons_dyad         -0.007    -0.007

#> powerdiff_dyad        858       838

The independent starts give nearly the same focal estimates. That is more informative than one attractive trace plot, but it still does not prove convergence. A research analysis should use multiple chains as a routine diagnostic and align latent representations before comparing their coordinates.

uv_plot(gade_ame_r2, layout = "biplot")

This is a visualization of the rank-two sensitivity fit, not evidence that two dimensions are uniquely correct. Do not treat “left” and “right” as named scales. Axis signs are arbitrary, and the two axes can be reordered together with their diagonal weights. A general rotation need not preserve this symmetric eigenmodel when the weights differ. The stable object is the fitted pairwise affinity matrix. Interpret those fitted pairings, then check whether they align with outside information that was not used to fit the model.

10 Posterior Predictive Checks: What Each Latent Layer Buys

gof_plot(gade_srm, statistics = c("sd.rowmean", "trans.dep"))

The first check, sd.rowmean, is the standard deviation across organizations of their mean square-root cooperation count across partnerships. In ordinary language, it measures how uneven broad cooperation activity is across organizations. The second, trans.dep, is a standardized product of centered outcomes across connected triples. It summarizes whether high outcomes cluster in threes, but it is not the percentage of triples that close.

The additive SRM reproduces the uneven actor activity but misses the network’s triadic pattern. That is exactly what its formula implies: one actor effect changes every relationship involving that organization, but it cannot express a special affinity among a set of organizations.

gof_plot(gade_ame, statistics = c("sd.rowmean", "trans.dep"))
gof_columns <- c("sd.rowmean", "trans.dep")
gof_comparison <- rbind(observed = gade_srm$GOF[1, gof_columns], srm_median = apply(gade_srm$GOF[-1, gof_columns, drop = FALSE], 2, median), ame_r1_median = apply(gade_ame$GOF[-1, gof_columns, drop = FALSE], 2, median), ame_r2_median = apply(gade_ame_r2$GOF[-1, gof_columns, drop = FALSE], 2, median))
round(gof_comparison, 3)
#>               sd.rowmean trans.dep
#> observed           0.441     0.206
#> srm_median         0.411    -0.029
#> ame_r1_median      0.444     0.223
#> ame_r2_median      0.444     0.220

The observed uneven-activity statistic is about 0.44. All three fits reproduce it closely. The observed normalized triple-pattern statistic is about 0.21. In this symmetric network, the package’s transitivity and cycle-dependence checks are identical, so plotting both would duplicate the same evidence. The SRM generates a median near -0.03, while both AME ranks generate a median around 0.22. The one-factor AME is therefore the simplest fitted model here that reproduces both broad organization differences and the observed triple pattern.

One coding detail matters here. When more than two organizations participated in one claimed operation, the data construction records every pair among them. A single multi-organization operation can therefore create a triangle mechanically. The AME fit reproduces this third-order feature of the recorded network, but that does not by itself establish a separate friend-of-a-friend cooperation mechanism. A good check tells us what a fitted model can reproduce, not why that pattern arose or whether the model is true.

ImportantThe SRM and AME Inference Checklist
  1. State whether the network is directed or symmetric.
  2. Name the observational unit and the actors that repeat across dyads.
  3. Separate point-estimate movement from interval-width movement.
  4. Inspect the latent actor effects as quantities worth interpreting, but do not reify them.
  5. Ask whether omitted structure might be correlated with the predictor of interest.
  6. Treat AME as a way to model recoverable latent dependence, not as a guarantee of exogeneity.
  7. Check convergence and simulate from the fitted model before interpreting it.

11 From Continuous Latent Effects to Discrete Roles

The SRM gives every organization one continuous activity score. AME adds continuous profiles that help explain why particular pairs fit together. A stochastic blockmodel asks a different question: can we group organizations that show similar patterns of cooperation into a few relational roles? Those roles are patterns in the network, not necessarily real-world communities.

For the block analysis, we use the observed 31-organization cooperation network from the same study. One additional organization appears in the network matrix but not in the prepared regression table. The regression and block analyses therefore share a source and setting, but they are not nested fits to an identical analytic network. The regression uses square-root counts among 30 organizations with complete covariates. The blockmodel uses a binary indicator of any recorded cooperation among the 31 organizations with at least one observed cooperative relationship. Its periphery is the periphery among observed collaborators, not every armed organization active in Syria.

load("data/gade_blocks.rda")
gade_A <- 1L * (gadeData > 0)
diag(gade_A) <- 0L
checkpoint(actors = nrow(gade_A), cooperative_pairs = sum(gade_A) / 2, density = round(mean(gade_A[upper.tri(gade_A)]), 3))
#> ------------------------------------------------------------------
#> CHECKPOINT: actors = 31   |   cooperative_pairs = 86   |   density = 0.185
#> ------------------------------------------------------------------

The binary outcome asks whether an unordered organization pair recorded at least one claimed joint operation at any point from July 2012 through June 2015. It discards how many operations the pair recorded. Every probability below refers to that whole-period relationship, not to a single operation, a future alliance, or the probability that two organizations share long-term goals.

12 The Cross-Sectional Blockmodel

Let KK be the number of roles, let zi∈{1,…,K}z_i\in\{1,\ldots,K\} be organization ii’s role, and let θgh\theta_{gh} be the probability of a recorded tie between an organization in role gg and one in role hh. Then

Yij∣zi,zj∼Bernoulli(θzizj). Y_{ij} \mid z_i,z_j \sim \operatorname{Bernoulli}(\theta_{z_i z_j}).

The central quantity is the matrix 𝛉\boldsymbol\theta, which collects all of those role-to-role probabilities. Its diagonal describes cooperation within roles; its off-diagonal describes cooperation across roles. A block is not necessarily a community. A core-periphery system has a dense core, extensive core-to-periphery ties, and a sparse periphery.

12.1 How Variational Expectation-Maximization Learns the Roles

Variational expectation-maximization (EM) alternates between two connected jobs.

  1. Start with tentative probabilities that each organization occupies each role.
  2. Use those probabilities to update the cooperation rate for every role pairing.
  3. Use the new cooperation rates to update each organization’s role probabilities.
  4. Keep alternating until the approximate fit stops improving.
  5. Repeat from several starting points and for several values of KK.

This approach is fast because it uses an approximation rather than drawing repeatedly from a posterior distribution. The estimated role probabilities can look more certain than they should, so multiple starts, nearby values of KK, and alternative specifications remain part of the analysis.

set.seed(6886)
gade_sbm <- BM_bernoulli("SBM_sym", gade_A, verbosity = 0, plotting = "")
gade_sbm$estimate()
plot(seq_along(gade_sbm$ICL), gade_sbm$ICL, type = "b", pch = 19, xlab = "number of blocks K", ylab = "ICL", main = "Syrian cooperation: choosing K")
K_gade <- which.max(gade_sbm$ICL)
K_gade
#> [1] 2
round(gade_sbm$ICL, 1)
#> [1] -225.7 -186.2 -189.8 -198.7

The integrated completed likelihood (ICL) rewards fit while penalizing unnecessary roles, and larger values are preferred here. ICL prefers two roles, but the three-role solution is close enough to inspect. The right conclusion is not that nature contains exactly two types. The two-role model gives the clearest balance between simplicity and fit, while the periphery can be divided more finely. As a stability check, ten additional random seeds all select two roles and recover the same ANF-ASIM core.

Check ten additional random starts 
check_block_seed <- function(seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  fit <- BM_bernoulli("SBM_sym", gade_A, verbosity = 0, plotting = "")
  invisible(capture.output(fit$estimate()))
  selected_k <- which.max(fit$ICL)
  z <- apply(fit$memberships[[selected_k]]$Z, 1, which.max)
  names(z) <- rownames(gade_A)
  theta <- fit$model_parameters[[selected_k]]$pi
  core <- which.max(rowMeans(theta))
  data.frame(seed = seed, selected_k = selected_k, anf_asim_core = ifelse(identical(sort(names(z)[z == core]), c("ANF", "ASIM")), "yes", "no"))
}
block_seed_check <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:10, check_block_seed))
block_seed_check
seed selected_k anf_asim_core
1 2 yes
2 2 yes
3 2 yes
4 2 yes
5 2 yes
6 2 yes
7 2 yes
8 2 yes
9 2 yes
10 2 yes 
z_gade <- apply(gade_sbm$memberships[[K_gade]]$Z, 1, which.max)
names(z_gade) <- rownames(gade_A)
split(names(z_gade), z_gade)
#> $`1`
#>  [1] "101st"  "13th"   "AARB"   "AF"     "ISIL"   "AASB"   "ADF"    "AASG"  
#>  [9] "ARC"    "LF"     "ATB"    "JAI"    "AFB"    "1st"    "AIG"    "FSIM"  
#> [17] "Hazm"   "JAA"    "LH"     "SAS"    "AALS"   "ASB"    "FKUG"   "MSC"   
#> [25] "ASL"    "NADAZM" "SRF"    "JMA"    "IARB"  
#> 
#> $`2`
#> [1] "ANF"  "ASIM"
theta_gade <- gade_sbm$model_parameters[[K_gade]]$pi
core_block <- which.max(rowMeans(theta_gade))
periphery_block <- setdiff(seq_len(K_gade), core_block)
block_order <- c(core_block, periphery_block)
theta_ordered <- theta_gade[block_order, block_order, drop = FALSE]
dimnames(theta_ordered) <- list(c("core", "periphery"), c("core", "periphery"))
core_actors <- names(z_gade)[z_gade == core_block]
periphery_actors <- names(z_gade)[z_gade == periphery_block]
within_core <- gade_A[core_actors, core_actors, drop = FALSE]
within_core <- within_core[upper.tri(within_core)]
core_periphery <- gade_A[core_actors, periphery_actors, drop = FALSE]
within_periphery <- gade_A[periphery_actors, periphery_actors, drop = FALSE]
within_periphery <- within_periphery[upper.tri(within_periphery)]
cell_summary <- function(x, fitted) c(observed_ties = sum(x), possible_pairs = length(x), observed_rate = mean(x), fitted_probability = fitted)
block_cell_summary <- rbind(
  "Core to core" = cell_summary(within_core, theta_ordered["core", "core"]),
  "Core to periphery" = cell_summary(core_periphery, theta_ordered["core", "periphery"]),
  "Periphery to periphery" = cell_summary(within_periphery, theta_ordered["periphery", "periphery"])
)
round(block_cell_summary, 3)
#>                        observed_ties possible_pairs observed_rate
#> Core to core                       1              1         1.000
#> Core to periphery                 44             58         0.759
#> Periphery to periphery            41            406         0.101
#>                        fitted_probability
#> Core to core                        0.959
#> Core to periphery                   0.730
#> Periphery to periphery              0.101

Al-Nusrah Front (ANF) and Ahrar al-Sham Islamic Movement (ASIM) form the two-organization core. The fitted within-core probability is about 0.96, but that number is supported by only one possible within-core pair, and ANF-ASIM is tied. The stronger evidence is the much broader cross-cell pattern: the two core organizations connect to 44 of 58 possible core-periphery pairs, while peripheral organizations connect to only 41 of 406 possible pairs among themselves.

In ordinary language, two organizations with different Islamist projects formed a small tactical backbone with links across much of this observed cooperation network. They worked with one another and reached many organizations that rarely cooperated among themselves. That does not make them a unified coalition or imply shared long-term goals. It is a core-periphery description of recorded tactical reach, not a map of two mutually isolated ideological camps.

The standard SBM has no separate parameter for each organization’s number of partners. It may therefore be grouping organizations mainly by how broadly they cooperate, turning the continuous activity difference from the SRM into two categories. ANF and ASIM appearing prominently in both models is not separate proof that they form a natural type. The useful cross-model finding is simpler: these two organizations have unusually broad tactical reach, while the exact description of that reach depends on the model.

12.2 Check the Nearby Three-Block Solution

ANF and ASIM remain together in the core. The additional block divides the periphery into organizations with moderate access to the core and organizations with weaker access. That is the stable result: the two-organization core persists, while the exact number of peripheral types is less certain.

12.3 Simulate Networks From the Fitted Roles

calc_block_gof <- function(M) c(degree_sd = sd(rowSums(M)), triangles = sum(diag(M %*% M %*% M)) / 6)
sim_gade_sbm <- function() {
  P <- theta_gade[z_gade, z_gade]
  M <- matrix(rbinom(length(P), 1, P), nrow(P), ncol(P))
  M[lower.tri(M)] <- t(M)[lower.tri(M)]
  diag(M) <- 0
  M
}
set.seed(6886)
gade_obs_gof <- calc_block_gof(gade_A)
gade_sim_gof <- t(replicate(500, calc_block_gof(sim_gade_sbm())))
round(rbind(observed = gade_obs_gof, simulated_mean = colMeans(gade_sim_gof), standardized_gap = abs(gade_obs_gof - colMeans(gade_sim_gof)) / apply(gade_sim_gof, 2, sd)), 2)
#>                  degree_sd triangles
#> observed              5.43     99.00
#> simulated_mean        4.72     61.32
#> standardized_gap      1.91      2.70

This check holds the chosen roles and fitted role-to-role probabilities fixed, simulates networks, and compares them with the observed network. It does not refit the model for every simulation or include uncertainty about the roles and probabilities. The simulated networks have slightly too little variation in how many partners organizations have and substantially too few triangles. The two-role model captures the broad core-periphery pattern, but it misses some smaller coalition structure. A degree-corrected blockmodel or continuous AME factors can represent more variation among organizations assigned to the same role.

The operation coding matters here too. A claimed operation involving three or more organizations becomes every pair among those organizations, so one multi-organization operation mechanically creates a triangle. The triangle gap can reflect coalition structure, variation within blocks, and the way operations were converted into ties. It is not a clean test of a friend-of-a-friend mechanism.

13 One Binary Panel, Two Longitudinal Questions

The cross-sectional Syrian analysis asks what organizes one observed network. We now use 13 annual Integrated Crisis Early Warning System (ICEWS) networks from 2002 through 2014 and fit two longitudinal models to the same binary outcome.

  • The longitudinal SRM asks which states repeatedly appear on the source and target sides of high-volume coded material conflict after regime difference and year-to-year density changes enter.
  • The repeated-network NetMix model asks how states’ estimated relational profiles differ across the annual networks.

ICEWS records coded events with a source actor and a target actor (Boschee et al. 2015). Our directed outcome equals one when ICEWS records more than 20 material-conflict events with state ii as the source and state jj as the target in a year. This is a relatively high event-volume threshold for our classroom panel. It is not a standard definition of war intensity, and the source-target distinction does not always correspond to military initiation and victimization. Event volume can also reflect sustained activity, news visibility, and source coverage. We keep the threshold fixed across the two main models, then check nearby thresholds after the SRM fit.

icews <- readRDS("data/icews.rds")
monadic_coverage <- unique(icews[, c("i", "year", "i_polity2", "i_log_gdp")])
coverage_counts <- aggregate(cbind(polity_years = as.integer(!is.na(i_polity2)), gdp_years = as.integer(!is.na(i_log_gdp))) ~ i, monadic_coverage, sum)
eligible_states <- coverage_counts$i[coverage_counts$polity_years == 13 & coverage_counts$gdp_years == 13]
conflict_totals <- aggregate(matlConf ~ i, icews, sum)
conflict_totals <- conflict_totals[conflict_totals$i %in% eligible_states, ]
states <- head(conflict_totals$i[order(conflict_totals$matlConf, decreasing = TRUE)], 18)
states
#>  [1] "United States"             "Israel"                   
#>  [3] "Russian Federation"        "Pakistan"                 
#>  [5] "India"                     "United Kingdom"           
#>  [7] "Iran, Islamic Republic Of" "China"                    
#>  [9] "France"                    "Japan"                    
#> [11] "Syrian Arab Republic"      "Thailand"                 
#> [13] "Australia"                 "Egypt"                    
#> [15] "Korea, Republic Of"        "Spain"                    
#> [17] "Indonesia"                 "Germany"
icews_sub <- icews[icews$i %in% states & icews$j %in% states, ]
icews_sub$high_event_volume <- as.integer(icews_sub$matlConf > 20)
icews_sub$polity_gap <- abs(icews_sub$i_polity2 - icews_sub$j_polity2) / 20
icews_sub$same_region <- as.integer(icews_sub$i_region == icews_sub$j_region)
netmix_dyad <- icews_sub[, c("i", "j", "year", "matlConf", "high_event_volume", "polity_gap", "same_region")]
names(netmix_dyad)[1:4] <- c("source", "target", "year", "material_conflict_events")
netmix_dyad$year <- as.integer(netmix_dyad$year)
netmix_monad <- unique(icews_sub[, c("i", "year")])
names(netmix_monad) <- c("state", "year")
netmix_monad$year <- as.integer(netmix_monad$year)
checkpoint(dyad_years = nrow(netmix_dyad), state_years = nrow(netmix_monad), years = length(unique(netmix_dyad$year)), states = length(states), above_threshold_rate = round(mean(netmix_dyad$high_event_volume), 3))
#> ------------------------------------------------------------------
#> CHECKPOINT: dyad_years = 3978   |   state_years = 234   |   years = 13   |   states = 18   |   above_threshold_rate = 0.218
#> ------------------------------------------------------------------

The 18 states are the highest-volume ICEWS sources among states with complete Polity and GDP coverage for all 13 years. Polity runs from -10 for a strongly autocratic regime to 10 for a strongly democratic regime. We use the absolute difference between two states’ scores and divide it by 20, so the model variable runs from 0 to 1. A 10-point difference on the original scale therefore enters the model as 0.5. We require complete Polity and GDP coverage to preserve one fixed case set for optional predictor extensions, although only Polity gap enters the displayed SRM and neither predictor enters the role-only NetMix fit. GDP completeness is a classroom design choice, not an estimator requirement. This purposive, outcome-selected case set gives the role model enough above-threshold relationships to learn from. It is not a probability sample of the international system. Every result below is conditional on this constructed high-information system, and its event rate should not be generalized to all states or presented as the published estimate in Olivella, Pratt, and Imai (2022).

14 A Fast Binary Longitudinal SRM

For state ii, state jj, and year tt, introduce a latent probit score:

Yijt*=αt+𝐱ijt𝖳𝛃+ai+bj+eijt,Yijt=𝟙(Yijt*>0),eijt∼N(0,1). Y^*_{ijt}=\alpha_t+\mathbf{x}_{ijt}^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta+a_i+b_j+e_{ijt}, \qquad Y_{ijt}=\mathbb{1}(Y^*_{ijt}>0), \qquad e_{ijt}\sim N(0,1).

(aibi)∼iidN[(00),(σa2σabσabσb2)],Corr(eijt,ejit)=ρ. \begin{pmatrix}a_i\\b_i\end{pmatrix} \stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} N\!\left[ \begin{pmatrix}0\\0\end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix}\sigma_a^2&\sigma_{ab}\\\sigma_{ab}&\sigma_b^2\end{pmatrix} \right], \qquad \operatorname{Corr}(e_{ijt},e_{jit})=\rho.

The indicator 𝟙(⋅)\mathbb{1}(\cdot) equals one when the latent score is above zero. The vector 𝐱ijt\mathbf x_{ijt} contains the measured dyad-year predictors, and 𝛃\boldsymbol\beta contains their coefficients. The residual variance is fixed to one because only the sign of the hidden score is observed. The year intercepts αt\alpha_t give each year its own overall baseline. The source-side effects aia_i and target-side effects bjb_j describe persistent state positions across all 13 annual networks. In the hierarchical target model, σab\sigma_{ab} asks whether states with high source-side activity also tend to have high target-side exposure, while ρ\rho describes the leftover connection between the two directions of the same pair in the same year.

The equations above state the full hierarchical probit SRM we have in mind. The fast alternating least-squares (ALS) fit below takes a more limited point-estimation route. It directly estimates the coefficients and additive state scores with iteratively reweighted probit updates. It does not draw from the joint normal hierarchy. The reported source-target covariance and reciprocal-residual correlation are empirical summaries of the fitted state scores and fitted working residuals, not posterior estimates of σab\sigma_{ab} and ρ\rho with uncertainty intervals.

This is a longitudinal model because it uses the complete dyad-year panel jointly, but it is intentionally pooled. Actor effects do not change every year. There is no dyad random effect, lagged-tie term, or residual serial-dependence process connecting the same pair across years. Year indicators absorb aggregate annual density changes, not relationship persistence.

14.1 Build the Matrix Lists lame() Expects

years <- sort(unique(netmix_dyad$year))
n_states <- length(states)
make_icews_matrix <- function(dd, value) {
  M <- acast(dd, factor(source, levels = states) ~ factor(target, levels = states), value.var = value)
  rownames(M) <- colnames(M) <- states
  diag(M) <- NA
  M
}
Y_icews <- lapply(years, function(tt) make_icews_matrix(netmix_dyad[netmix_dyad$year == tt, ], "high_event_volume"))
names(Y_icews) <- years
x_names <- c("polity_gap", "same_region", paste0("year_", years[-1]))
X_icews <- lapply(seq_along(years), function(tt) {
  dd <- netmix_dyad[netmix_dyad$year == years[tt], ]
  A <- array(NA_real_, dim = c(n_states, n_states, length(x_names)), dimnames = list(states, states, x_names))
  A[, , "polity_gap"] <- make_icews_matrix(dd, "polity_gap")
  A[, , "same_region"] <- make_icews_matrix(dd, "same_region")
  for (kk in seq_along(years[-1])) {
    A[, , paste0("year_", years[-1][kk])] <- 1L * (tt == kk + 1L)
    diag(A[, , paste0("year_", years[-1][kk])]) <- NA
  }
  A
})
names(X_icews) <- years

14.2 Use the Fast Point Estimator Today

icews_srm_als <- cache_fit("icews_binary_lame_als_volume20_v2", lame(
  Y = Y_icews, Xdyad = X_icews,
  family = "binary", symmetric = FALSE, R = 0,
  method = "als", als_max_iter = 500,
  verbose = FALSE
))
checkpoint(converged = icews_srm_als$converged, iterations = icews_srm_als$iterations, deviance = round(icews_srm_als$deviance, 1))
#> ------------------------------------------------------------------
#> CHECKPOINT: converged = TRUE   |   iterations = 8   |   deviance = 3339.9
#> ------------------------------------------------------------------

method = "als" is the fast, MCMC-free route. We already did the baby Bayesian and MCMC introduction today, so alternating least squares gets its own introduction next time. For now, the high-level idea is enough: begin with provisional regression and actor effects, update one block while holding the others fixed, cycle through the blocks, and stop when the fitted values stabilize. The binary updates use an iteratively reweighted probit approximation.

ALS returns an approximate point fit, not posterior draws. There are no credible intervals in this output. A paper can add bootstrap intervals or use MCMC after the specification has been developed. Today we use ALS to see the longitudinal structure quickly and label the result as exploratory point estimation.

srm_probability_contrasts <- data.frame(contrast = c("average discrete contrast: same_region 0 versus 1", "average discrete contrast: Polity gap 0 versus 10 points"), probability_before = c(mean(p_same0), mean(p_gap0)), probability_after = c(mean(p_same1), mean(p_gap50)))

#> actor_source_target_correlation     residual_dyadic_reciprocity 
#>                           0.928                           0.182

The coefficient signs become easier to understand after translating the probit scale into probabilities. We score the same fitted dyad-years once with same_region = 0 and once with same_region = 1, while keeping their fitted state scores, years, and Polity gaps fixed. The average fitted probability rises from about 17% to 45%, a difference of about 28 percentage points. Repeating the exercise for a Polity gap of 0 versus 10 points on the original scale changes the average from about 17% to 24%, a difference of about 7 points. These are model-based comparisons, not observed group differences or changes within the same pair. ALS supplies no uncertainty interval for either comparison, and neither is a causal effect.

After accounting for region, Polity difference, and year, the United States has the largest fitted source-side and target-side scores. Israel, Iran, the United Kingdom, Pakistan, India, and Russia appear near the top of one or both rankings. This may reflect geopolitical centrality, but ICEWS is built from coded news events, so media attention and source coverage are also plausible contributors. The fitted source-side and target-side state scores correlate at about 0.93: states that appear unusually often as coded sources also tend to appear unusually often as coded targets. The correlation between fitted working residuals for the two directions of the same pair is much smaller, about 0.18. Both numbers are descriptive correlations calculated from fitted point quantities. They are not posterior parameter estimates and have no uncertainty intervals here.

icews_ab <- rbind(data.frame(state = names(icews_srm_als$a), effect = icews_srm_als$a, type = "Source-side above-threshold propensity"), data.frame(state = names(icews_srm_als$b), effect = icews_srm_als$b, type = "Target-side above-threshold propensity"))
ggplot(icews_ab, aes(effect, reorder(state, effect))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey70") +
  geom_point(color = "#18453B", size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~ type, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Pooled adjusted actor effect, point estimate", y = NULL)

Because the fast ALS fit has no uncertainty intervals, treat the rankings as exploratory. “Largest” means largest point estimate in this selected 18-state system, not a known population ranking.

WarningScope of This Fast Longitudinal SRM

Each state keeps the same source-side and target-side score in every year, so do not call this a model of changing state positions. The model allows the overall event rate to differ by year, but it does not give each state pair its own long-run baseline, ask whether last year’s outcome predicts this year’s, or directly model leftover dependence over time. A dynamic SRM would allow the state scores to change through a specified time process and would require its own stability and uncertainty checks.

14.4 Does the Event-Volume Threshold Drive the Result?

fit_threshold_srm <- function(cutoff) {
  Y_cut <- lapply(years, function(tt) {
    dd <- netmix_dyad[netmix_dyad$year == tt, ]
    dd$threshold_outcome <- as.integer(dd$material_conflict_events > cutoff)
    make_icews_matrix(dd, "threshold_outcome")
  })
  names(Y_cut) <- years
  cache_fit(paste0("icews_binary_lame_als_volume", cutoff, "_v1"), lame(
    Y = Y_cut, Xdyad = X_icews,
    family = "binary", symmetric = FALSE, R = 0,
    method = "als", als_max_iter = 500,
    verbose = FALSE
  ))
}
threshold_fits <- list("10" = fit_threshold_srm(10), "20" = icews_srm_als, "30" = fit_threshold_srm(30))
threshold_summary <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(threshold_fits), function(cutoff) {
  fit <- threshold_fits[[cutoff]]
  data.frame(
    threshold = as.integer(cutoff),
    outcome_rate = mean(netmix_dyad$material_conflict_events > as.integer(cutoff)),
    polity_gap = unname(fit$coefficients["polity_gap_dyad"]),
    same_region = unname(fit$coefficients["same_region_dyad"]),
    actor_correlation = unname(fit$VC["cab"] / sqrt(fit$VC["va"] * fit$VC["vb"])),
    row.names = NULL
  )
}))
threshold_summary[-1] <- round(threshold_summary[-1], 3)
threshold_summary
threshold outcome_rate polity_gap same_region actor_correlation
10 0.322 0.858 1.281 0.910
20 0.218 0.827 1.290 0.928
30 0.158 1.195 1.504 0.897

Moving the threshold from 10 to 20 to 30 coded events changes the number of positive dyad-years and the magnitude of the point estimates, as it should. The positive Polity-gap and same-region patterns, along with a strong source-target actor correlation, survive all three choices. This does not make the threshold correct or the associations causal. It shows that the main classroom interpretation is not an artifact of exactly 20 events.

15 Repeated-Network Role Mixtures With NetMix

The question now changes. Instead of asking which states repeatedly sit above or below a measured prediction, we ask what each state’s pattern of relationships looks like in each year. The main NetMix specification fixes the number of roles at two in advance, then learns both role patterns from the observed relationships. Every state-year receives two weights showing how closely its relationships resemble those learned roles. A state can partly resemble both. We leave predictors out of this first fit so we can see what the role pattern itself is doing.

15.1 What NetMix Is Trying to Learn

  1. A two-by-two matrix records how often each source-role and target-role pairing crosses the event threshold.
  2. Every state-year receives two role weights that add to one.
  3. Those weights are estimated separately by year without forcing a state into one permanent category.

For each dyad-year, imagine drawing a source role gg from state ii’s membership vector 𝛑it\boldsymbol\pi_{it} and a target role hh from state jj’s membership vector 𝛑jt\boldsymbol\pi_{jt}:

gijt∼Categorical(𝛑it),hijt∼Categorical(𝛑jt),Yijt∣gijt,hijt∼Bernoulli(θgijt,hijt). g_{ijt}\sim\operatorname{Categorical}(\boldsymbol\pi_{it}), \qquad h_{ijt}\sim\operatorname{Categorical}(\boldsymbol\pi_{jt}), \qquad Y_{ijt}\mid g_{ijt},h_{ijt}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\theta_{g_{ijt},h_{ijt}}).

After averaging over those latent role draws, the fitted dyad-year probability is

Pr(Yijt=1∣𝛑it,𝛑jt,𝚯)=∑g∑hπit,gπjt,hθgh=𝛑it𝖳𝚯𝛑jt. \Pr(Y_{ijt}=1\mid\boldsymbol\pi_{it},\boldsymbol\pi_{jt},\boldsymbol\Theta) =\sum_g\sum_h\pi_{it,g}\pi_{jt,h}\theta_{gh} =\boldsymbol\pi_{it}^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\Theta\boldsymbol\pi_{jt}.

The four entries of 𝚯\boldsymbol\Theta are probabilities for hypothetical state-years that fully match one role. A real state-year generally mixes both roles, so its fitted dyadic probability is a weighted average of all four entries.

netmix_seeds <- 1:20
netmix_candidates <- cache_fit("netmix_icews_batch_k2_volume20_v2", lapply(netmix_seeds, function(s) NetMix::mmsbm(
  high_event_volume ~ 1,
  ~ 1,
  senderID = "source", receiverID = "target", nodeID = "state", timeID = "year",
  data.dyad = netmix_dyad, data.monad = netmix_monad,
  n.blocks = 2, n.hmmstates = 1, directed = TRUE,
  mmsbm.control = list(seed = s, nstart = 10, svi = FALSE, vi_iter = 15000, conv_tol = 1e-3, hessian = FALSE, assortative = FALSE, mu_block = c(-2.5, -1.5), verbose = FALSE)
)))
netmix_elbo <- vapply(netmix_candidates, function(x) x$LowerBound, numeric(1))
summarize_netmix_run <- function(x) {
  P <- plogis(x$BlockModel)
  active <- which.max(rowMeans(P) + colMeans(P))
  quiet <- setdiff(seq_len(nrow(P)), active)
  c(quiet_quiet = P[quiet, quiet], mixed = mean(c(P[quiet, active], P[active, quiet])), active_active = P[active, active])
}
netmix_run_summary <- data.frame(seed = netmix_seeds, final_elbo = netmix_elbo, t(vapply(netmix_candidates, summarize_netmix_run, numeric(3))))
netmix_run_summary <- netmix_run_summary[order(netmix_run_summary$final_elbo, decreasing = TRUE), ]
head(round(netmix_run_summary, 3), 10)
seed final_elbo quiet_quiet mixed active_active

6 6 -234.657 0.050 0.846 0.966
13 13 -234.659 0.050 0.846 0.966
8 8 -234.661 0.050 0.846 0.966

netmix_long <- netmix_candidates[[which.max(netmix_elbo)]]

We fix KK, the number of roles, at two in advance so the classroom result remains easy to inspect. NetMix then learns what those two role patterns look like. The nine best runs recover essentially the same role-to-role probabilities after matching the otherwise arbitrary role labels. The other runs stop at clearly worse approximate fit scores. The result therefore does not look like an accident of one starting value. This check applies only to the chosen two-role model; it does not show that two is the correct number of roles.

The argument n.hmmstates = 1 is easy to misread. In NetMix, one hidden state means there is no hidden Markov model. The fit estimates a separate membership vector for every state-year and shares one role matrix across years, but it does not estimate transition probabilities or smooth a state’s memberships over time. The full NetMix framework can fit those dynamics; this fast classroom specification does not.

15.2 How the Fast NetMix Estimator Works

NetMix uses full-batch variational inference here. It begins with tentative role weights, updates which weights best fit each state-year, re-estimates how often each role pairing crosses the event threshold, and repeats until the evidence lower bound (ELBO) stops improving. The ELBO is the approximate fit score the algorithm tries to increase. This is a fast approximation rather than an MCMC sample.

This 18-state system is small enough that full-batch updates are faster and more stable than stochastic subsampling. NetMix also offers stochastic variational inference for larger networks, where each iteration updates only a sample of nodes. Both routes are approximate and can settle at local optima, so multiple starts, role-label alignment, and calibration remain necessary. hessian = FALSE keeps this a descriptive point fit without standard errors.

c(converged = netmix_long$converged, iterations = netmix_long$niter, final_elbo = netmix_long$LowerBound)
#>  converged iterations final_elbo 
#>     1.0000   100.0000  -234.6401

15.3 Read the Block Matrix Before Naming the Roles

netmix_theta_raw <- plogis(netmix_long$BlockModel)
active_role <- which.max(rowMeans(netmix_theta_raw) + colMeans(netmix_theta_raw))
quiet_role <- setdiff(seq_len(nrow(netmix_theta_raw)), active_role)
netmix_role_order <- c(quiet_role, active_role)
netmix_theta <- netmix_theta_raw[netmix_role_order, netmix_role_order, drop = FALSE]
dimnames(netmix_theta) <- list(source_role = c("lower involvement", "broad event involvement"), target_role = c("lower involvement", "broad event involvement"))
round(netmix_theta, 2)
#>                          target_role
#> source_role               lower involvement broad event involvement
#>   lower involvement                    0.05                    0.83
#>   broad event involvement              0.86                    0.97

Read rows as source roles and columns as target roles. For hypothetical state-years that fully match the lower-involvement role, the fitted probability is about 0.05. It is about 0.83 or 0.86 when one side fully matches each role, and about 0.97 when both sides fully match the broadly involved role. Actual state-years usually mix the two roles, so their fitted dyad-year probability averages all four cells using their role weights.

15.4 Compare Annual Membership Profiles With Observed Breadth

membership_long <- data.frame(key = colnames(netmix_long$MixedMembership), t(netmix_long$MixedMembership), check.names = FALSE)
names(membership_long)[-1] <- paste0("Group ", seq_len(netmix_long$n_blocks))
membership_long$state <- sub("@[0-9]+$", "", membership_long$key)
membership_long$year <- as.integer(sub("^.*@", "", membership_long$key))
membership_long$broad_role_membership <- membership_long[[paste0("Group ", active_role)]]
source_breadth <- aggregate(high_event_volume ~ source + year, netmix_dyad, mean)
names(source_breadth) <- c("state", "year", "source_breadth")
target_breadth <- aggregate(high_event_volume ~ target + year, netmix_dyad, mean)
names(target_breadth) <- c("state", "year", "target_breadth")
membership_long <- merge(membership_long, source_breadth, by = c("state", "year"), all.x = TRUE)
membership_long <- merge(membership_long, target_breadth, by = c("state", "year"), all.x = TRUE)
membership_long$observed_breadth <- (membership_long$source_breadth + membership_long$target_breadth) / 2
membership_breadth_correlations <- c(
  source = cor(membership_long$broad_role_membership, membership_long$source_breadth),
  target = cor(membership_long$broad_role_membership, membership_long$target_breadth),
  combined = cor(membership_long$broad_role_membership, membership_long$observed_breadth)
)
round(membership_breadth_correlations, 3)
#>   source   target combined 
#>    0.923    0.921    0.953
focus_states <- c("Syrian Arab Republic", "Russian Federation", "Iran, Islamic Republic Of", "Pakistan", "United States", "Israel")
profile_long <- melt(membership_long[membership_long$state %in% focus_states, ], id.vars = c("state", "year"), measure.vars = c("broad_role_membership", "observed_breadth"), variable.name = "measure", value.name = "value")
profile_long$measure <- factor(profile_long$measure, levels = c("broad_role_membership", "observed_breadth"), labels = c("NetMix broad-role membership", "Observed source-target breadth"))
ggplot(profile_long, aes(year, value, color = measure, linetype = measure)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = .9) +
  geom_point(size = 1.3) +
  facet_wrap(~ state) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#18453B", "#7BBD00")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Annual relational profile", color = NULL, linetype = NULL)

The broad-role weight correlates about 0.95 with a simple observed quantity: the share of possible source-side and target-side relationships that cross the threshold. In this application, the role mostly summarizes how widely a state appears in high-volume coded relationships during a year. It is not a hidden ideological, alliance, or geopolitical camp.

The United States remains strongly associated with broad involvement throughout the panel. Syria’s annual membership is near zero through 2010, rises in 2011, reaches about 0.37 in 2012, and remains elevated through 2014 as the number of selected states connected to it by above-threshold relationships widens. These annual estimates line up with recognizable historical periods, but they are not a learned transition path or an explanation of the Syrian civil war. System-wide density shifts and ICEWS coverage can also move the profiles because this role-only model has no year intercept.

15.5 In-Sample Reconstruction Check

netmix_mm <- t(netmix_long$MixedMembership)
netmix_dd <- netmix_long$dyadic.data
sender_key <- paste(netmix_dd[["(sid)"]], netmix_dd[["(tid)"]], sep = "@")
receiver_key <- paste(netmix_dd[["(rid)"]], netmix_dd[["(tid)"]], sep = "@")
sender_mm <- netmix_mm[match(sender_key, rownames(netmix_mm)), , drop = FALSE]
receiver_mm <- netmix_mm[match(receiver_key, rownames(netmix_mm)), , drop = FALSE]
netmix_pred <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(netmix_dd)), function(ii) sum(outer(sender_mm[ii, ], receiver_mm[ii, ]) * netmix_theta_raw), numeric(1))
calibration <- data.frame(observed = netmix_long$Y, predicted = netmix_pred)
calibration$bin <- cut(calibration$predicted, quantile(calibration$predicted, probs = seq(0, 1, .2), na.rm = TRUE), include.lowest = TRUE, labels = c("lowest", "second", "third", "fourth", "highest"))
aggregate(cbind(observed, predicted) ~ bin, calibration, mean)
bin observed predicted
lowest 0.0138191 0.0784206
second 0.0742138 0.0962294
third 0.1469849 0.1482782
fourth 0.2402516 0.2315161
highest 0.6143216 0.5679937 
brier_model <- mean((calibration$observed - calibration$predicted)^2)
brier_null <- mean((calibration$observed - mean(calibration$observed))^2)
round(c(role_model = brier_model, constant_probability = brier_null), 3)
#>           role_model constant_probability 
#>                0.115                0.170

Sort the dyad-years into five equal groups from lowest to highest fitted probability. The observed above-threshold rate is about 0.01 in the lowest group and about 0.61 in the highest. The Brier score is the average squared difference between a predicted probability and the observed zero-or-one outcome, so lower is better. It is about 0.115 for the role model and 0.17 for one constant probability. The model still overpredicts the quietest dyads and underpredicts the most active ones. More importantly, the same dyad-years estimated the roles and probability matrix and were then scored here. This is an in-sample reconstruction check, not out-of-sample validation or forecasting evidence.

WarningWhat We Can and Cannot Claim

Within this chosen two-role model, we can describe how each state-year’s relationship pattern resembles the two roles. We cannot treat those roles as natural geopolitical kinds, read a role weight as the probability that a state is “in conflict,” claim that the model estimated transitions, compare role numbers across separate fits without matching them, or generalize from this selected event-rich case set to all states. A paper should compare thresholds, actor sets, role counts, hidden-state structures, starting values, and predictor specifications, then evaluate held-out dyads or years before making predictive claims.

16 How the Four Models Represent the Missing Pattern

Representation Latent quantity Best at Main limitation
Social relations model (SRM) One activity score per actor, or separate source-side and target-side scores Recurring broad actor involvement and reciprocity Cannot represent special affinity among particular groups of actors
Additive and multiplicative effects model (AME) Continuous hidden relational profiles Pair-specific patterns left after measured variables and actor activity enter The hidden dimensions need outside evidence before receiving labels
Stochastic blockmodel (SBM) One discrete relational role per actor A readable role-to-role cooperation pattern Actors in one role are treated as interchangeable unless the model is extended
Repeated-network mixed-membership stochastic blockmodel, fitted with NetMix A separate blend of roles for every actor-year, with one shared role matrix Comparing how annual relationship patterns differ With one hidden state, it has no transition process or smoothing across years

17 After the Models Run, Say What We Learned

For the Syrian cooperation application, a clear summary is:

Among these Syrian armed organizations, groups closer to one another in estimated size and groups operating in the same places carried out more recorded joint operations in the fitted models. The evidence also points toward more cooperation among ideologically similar groups, although that finding becomes less certain when the model allows a second unmeasured cooperation pattern.

ANF and ASIM stand out because they took part in more recorded joint operations across their partnerships than their measured characteristics would lead us to expect. When we look only at whether each pair ever cooperated, they connect to 44 of 58 possible core-periphery pairs, compared with 41 of 406 possible ties among peripheral organizations. Together they form a small tactical core with links across much of the otherwise fragmented network. That does not mean they shared the same long-term goals or formed a unified coalition.

These patterns describe this network and period. They do not show that ideology, relative power, or location caused cooperation.

For the longitudinal ICEWS application:

To make the model concrete, we use it twice on the same state-pair-years, leaving everything else as fitted. The average estimated chance of more than 20 coded conflict events is 17% when we set the pair to different-region and 45% when we set it to same-region. In a separate comparison, the average is 17% with a 0-point Polity gap and 24% with a 10-point gap.

The United States appears unusually often on both sides of these high-volume relationships across the 13 years. NetMix gives us a yearly summary: the United States remains connected to many different states, while Syria’s high-volume connections widen beginning in 2011.

These patterns may reflect real state involvement, news coverage, and coding practices. They do not measure conflict severity, establish causal effects, or show states moving through a fixed sequence of roles.

18 Exercises

  1. Inference: Let β=0.5\beta=0.5, γ=1\gamma=1, and z=αx+ez=\alpha x+e, where ee contains recurring actor effects. Compute the naive target when α=0.4\alpha=0.4, −0.4-0.4, and 00. Explain why the zero-correlation case can still have incorrect independent-row uncertainty.
  2. SRM: Inspect the eight largest and smallest gade_srm$APM values. Choose two organizations and write an interpretation that does not turn the latent effect into a fixed trait.
  3. AME: Compare the SRM and rank-one AME posterior predictive checks. Then compare the rank-one and rank-two ideology intervals. Which conclusion is stable, and which depends on rank?
  4. Blocks: Use the observed numerators and denominators to explain why the cross-cell evidence is stronger than the fitted core-core probability. Then compare the two- and three-block solutions.
  5. Longitudinal SRM: Compare thresholds of 10, 20, and 30 events. Which conclusions survive, and what still prevents a causal interpretation? As an extension, add GDP difference while retaining the common case set.
  6. NetMix: Compare raw source-side breadth, target-side breadth, and fitted membership for Syria, Russia, Iran, and the United States. Explain what the role adds without calling it a transition process or a geopolitical bloc.

19 Reading

  • Back and Kenny (2010), “The Social Relations Model: How to Understand Dyadic Processes,” for the core actor, partner, and relationship decomposition.
  • Hoff (2005), “Bilinear Mixed-Effects Models for Dyadic Data,” for the additive and multiplicative network regression framework.
  • Minhas, Hoff, and Ward (2019), “Inferential Approaches for Network Analysis: AMEN for Latent Factor Models,” for inference with additive and multiplicative effects.
  • Gade, Gabbay, Hafez, and Kelly (2019), “Networks of Cooperation: Rebel Alliances in Fragmented Civil Wars,” for the Syrian cooperation application used here.
  • Minhas et al. (2022), “Taking Dyads Seriously,” for the simulation evidence, applied reanalyses, latent-effect interpretation, and the correlated-omitted-variable limitation.
  • Holland, Laskey, and Leinhardt (1983), “Stochastic Blockmodels: First Steps,” for the generative blockmodel.
  • Karrer and Newman (2011), “Stochastic Blockmodels and Community Structure in Networks,” for degree-corrected blocks.
  • Boschee et al. (2015), “ICEWS Coded Event Data,” for the source-target event records used in the longitudinal classroom panel.
  • Olivella, Pratt, and Imai (2022), “Dynamic Stochastic Blockmodel Regression for Network Data,” for the broader dynamic mixed-membership framework and international-conflict application behind NetMix. Our one-hidden-state classroom fit deliberately does not estimate its HMM transition layer.
